topicName: Common Table Expressions (CTEs) and Window Functions
content:
[{"order":1,"type":"heading","text":"Advanced MySQL: Common Table Expressions (CTEs) and Window Functions"},{"order":2,"type":"paragraph","text":"Modern SQL provides powerful tools to simplify complex queries and perform advanced data analysis. Among the most impactful additions to MySQL (starting from version 8.0) are Common Table Expressions (CTEs) and Window Functions. This tutorial will guide you through understanding, writing, and combining these features to optimize your database workflows."},{"order":3,"type":"heading","text":"1. Understanding Common Table Expressions (CTEs)"},{"order":4,"type":"paragraph","text":"A Common Table Expression (CTE) is a named temporary result set that exists only within the execution scope of a single SQL statement. Think of it as a more readable, powerful alternative to subqueries and derived tables. CTEs are defined using the WITH keyword."},{"order":5,"type":"subheading","text":"Basic CTE Syntax"},{"order":6,"type":"code","text":"WITH cte_name AS (
    SELECT column1, column2
    FROM table_name
    WHERE condition
)
SELECT * FROM cte_name;"},{"order":7,"type":"subheading","text":"Recursive CTEs"},{"order":8,"type":"paragraph","text":"CTEs can also be recursive, meaning they reference themselves. This is particularly useful for traversing hierarchical data, such as organizational charts, bill of materials, or threaded comments."},{"order":9,"type":"code","text":"WITH RECURSIVE NumberSequence AS (
    SELECT 1 AS n
    UNION ALL
    SELECT n + 1 FROM NumberSequence WHERE n < 5
)
SELECT * FROM NumberSequence;"},{"order":10,"type":"heading","text":"2. Mastering Window Functions"},{"order":11,"type":"paragraph","text":"Unlike aggregate functions (which group multiple rows into a single summary row), window functions perform calculations across a set of table rows that are somehow related to the current row. They use the OVER() clause to define the window."},{"order":12,"type":"subheading","text":"Key Components of Window Functions"},{"order":13,"type":"bullet_point","text":"PARTITION BY: Divides the result set into partitions to which the function is applied."},{"order":14,"type":"bullet_point","text":"ORDER BY: Defines the logical order of the rows within each partition."},{"order":15,"type":"bullet_point","text":"ROWS / RANGE: Further limits the rows within the partition (the frame clause)."},{"order":16,"type":"subheading","text":"Common Window Functions"},{"order":17,"type":"code","text":"SELECT 
    employee_id, 
    department, 
    salary,
    ROW_NUMBER() OVER(PARTITION BY department ORDER BY salary DESC) AS row_num,
    RANK() OVER(PARTITION BY department ORDER BY salary DESC) AS rank_num,
    AVG(salary) OVER(PARTITION BY department) AS avg_dept_salary
FROM employees;"},{"order":18,"type":"heading","text":"3. Combining CTEs and Window Functions"},{"order":19,"type":"paragraph","text":"A common architectural pattern in modern analytics is using a CTE to aggregate or rank data using a window function, and then querying that CTE for final filtering. Window functions cannot be directly used in the WHERE clause, making CTEs the perfect wrapper."},{"order":20,"type":"code","text":"WITH RankedProducts AS (
    SELECT 
        product_id,
        category,
        price,
        ROW_NUMBER() OVER(PARTITION BY category ORDER BY price DESC) as price_rank
    FROM products
)
SELECT product_id, category, price
FROM RankedProducts
WHERE price_rank <= 3;"},{"order":21,"type":"heading","text":"Conclusion"},{"order":22,"type":"paragraph","text":"By mastering CTEs and window functions in MySQL, you can write cleaner, more maintainable, and highly efficient queries. These constructs reduce the need for complex self-joins and procedural code, keeping your analytics logic directly inside the database engine."}]
